title: Decode the evidence
text: The T02 live request used amount=5, category=17, difficulty=medium, type=boolean, and encode=url3986. Its recorded pair is shown immediately below this answer. ScienceQuestion.decode in lib/quiz.dart applies Uri.decodeComponent separately to category, question, correct_answer, and the single incorrect answer. That matches the endpoint's URL-component contract: percent escapes represent encoded bytes, including punctuation and UTF-8 characters. An HTML unescaper handles a different representation, such as ampersand entity names, and cannot replace decoding percent escapes. Decoding is followed by validation rather than treated as proof of a playable response. The category must become Science & Nature, the answer pair must be exactly True and False, and all five results must satisfy the metadata contract. T03 rejects malformed escapes, invalid UTF-8, nonzero API codes, and a four-result response. Invalid data enters requestError with a readable explanation. OpenTriviaSource.retryAfter enforces five seconds between user-triggered HTTP requests, including requests following failure.

title: Separate the write and verification outcomes
text: T09 deliberately makes two different observations about one document. FirestoreAttemptStore.commit finishes a real create-once transaction, so RoundController.writeAcknowledged becomes true. The one-shot development hook then rejects the first verification call with permission-denied. At that point verified remains null, reconciliationRequired remains true, and phase becomes permissionDenied. The amber card therefore says Write acknowledged; verification unavailable. Transaction acknowledgement supports the first clause; there is no successful server snapshot to support Cloud verified. Retry server verification calls _readOriginal with the same UID and round ID. It neither freezes a new score nor allocates another document. The subsequent real Source.server snapshot must exist, contain the exact six typed fields, have a resolved Timestamp, and report neither cache origin nor pending writes. Only that evidence sets verified and transitions to cloudVerified. T09's screenshots and server trace distinguish those moments. The local regression also counts one commit and two reads, making accidental duplicate submission observable.

title: Identity and collision
text: A retry identifies the same logical round through its original UID and roundId. The frozen score is captured only after all five selections are final. If another request uses that ID with a changed score, the transaction reads the existing record and compares all five non-timestamp fields. A mismatch raises collision; it does not update the original or replace its timestamp. G01 runs this competition through two independently authenticated clients and records the actual winner. The winning payload is the one present in the subsequent server-only read, rather than whichever client finished its UI work first. A genuinely new quiz is different: startRound allocates a new document ID, clears selections, resets progress, and fetches five questions. Replay is unavailable while the previous outcome is unresolved. T05 verifies that reset, while G02 checks that independent concurrent IDs retain their own scores. _current additionally binds asynchronous callbacks to generation, initiating UID, and round ID, preventing an old operation from changing a different user's screen.

title: Access is not truth
text: T10 signs a separate Firebase client in as test user B and attempts both a server read and a create under user A's path. The deployed owner rule rejects both with permission-denied. T11 separately checks score 6, an unexpected field, and an update, then reads A's original record to confirm that its score and timestamp remain unchanged. These checks establish authorization, shape validation, and immutability. They cannot establish honest scoring because an owner can write a fabricated integer between zero and five while satisfying every client-facing rule. A trusted scoring service would authenticate the Firebase ID token, issue a server-owned round with question identifiers, and accept one final answer set under an idempotency key. It would calculate the score from server-held answers and create the attempt atomically. Direct client creates would then be denied. Rate limits and expiry reduce abuse, but a backend still cannot prove who supplied an answer or prevent every form of outside assistance.

title: Critique the AI recovery proposal
text: The accompanying AI critique records the fictional prompt, OpenAI Codex as the tool, November 17, 2026 as the date, and the relevant response excerpt. Its useful recommendation is to preserve the committed ID and retry verification rather than describe a denied read as a failed save. T09 tests that claim with a real transaction and a real final server read; only the intervening denial is injected. The second tested claim concerns timeout uncertainty. The delayed-future regression proves that the ten-second UI deadline does not cancel the original operation. The initial wording does not specify lock ownership after timeout or protection against an authentication change. Those omissions matter because an unlocked retry can overlap the original future, and an unguarded completion can appear on another user's screen. The revised controller keeps operationActive tied to settlement, requires same-ID reconciliation, and checks _generation, UID, and round ID before every completion. G03 tests delivery of a stale real server response across an actual account switch.

title: Defend the recovery experience
text: Save failed would make an unsupported claim after an acknowledged transaction and encourage the user to create another attempt. Science Signal instead shows an amber cloud-sync icon, the explicit Write acknowledged; verification unavailable message, a readable error code, and the retained round-ID suffix. T09 captures this screen before the manual retry turns it green with Cloud verified and a resolved server timestamp. Text and icons carry meaning alongside color. Replay and sign-out stay disabled while unresolved, and the retry button names the operation it actually performs. The failed-first retrieval regression exposed a related clarity problem: reading another historical ID initially left the preceding quiz's review visible. The corrected retrieve method clears questions, selections, and index before reading the selected record. The passing regression prevents that misleading association. An alternative would poll the server automatically, reducing user effort but adding reads, latency uncertainty, and harder-to-explain recovery. A deliberate manual read keeps the action bounded and observable.

title: Competing operations and the observable winner
text: G01 uses two independently initialized Firebase applications, authentication sessions, and Firestore clients signed in as the same test user. Both receive the same document ID before either transaction begins; one frozen payload contains score one and the other score four. Each callback reads first. If both initially observe absence, Firestore can retry a conflicting transaction after the competing commit. The retried callback then compares the existing fixed fields and reports collision for the differing payload. The observable winner is the payload in the final Source.server snapshot with a resolved timestamp. It is not defined by callback entry, UI animation order, or which request was issued first. The G01 trace records the actual outcomes, and the competing-operation diagram shows the allowed interleaving. G02 changes the experiment by assigning independent IDs and scores zero and five. Both operations should succeed, and each read must return its initiating ID and score. This experiment justified keeping document references and immutable inputs local to each operation instead of placing a shared current-result variable inside the retryable callback. G03 extends isolation to identity changes by discarding a delayed response whose initiating generation no longer matches.

title: Authenticated server authoritative scoring
text: A stronger design would replace client-authored scores with an authenticated scoring endpoint. POST /rounds would validate a Firebase ID token and create a server-owned round identifier, an expiry, an owner UID, and the selected question identifiers. The server would retain the answer key and return only question prompts and permitted choices. POST /rounds/{id}/answers would accept one final answer set and an idempotency key, verify ownership and expiry, validate the exact question set, calculate the score, and atomically create the immutable result. Repeated identical requests would return the original attempt; a different answer set for the same completed round would return a conflict. Direct Firestore creates from mobile clients would be denied, while owner reads would remain permitted. T10 and T11 demonstrate why identity and schema enforcement are necessary; their limits motivate moving scoring across the trust boundary. Replay protection needs a server-stored completion state or request digest, not just a client-generated nonce. Remaining threats include account sharing, leaked questions, automated solving, stolen tokens, and denial of service. Rate limits, token verification, short expiries, audit trails, and carefully scoped administrative access reduce those threats without claiming to prove quiz honesty.

title: Transactions and backend idempotency
text: Science Signal's create-once client transaction reads one exact document, creates it only when absent, and follows acknowledgement with a separate server-only confirmation read. That is a compact architecture without an additional deployed service. It still consumes document reads, writes, network round trips, and potentially repeated reads under contention. G01 makes that contention observable: competing payloads at one ID produce one winner and one collision. G02 shows that unrelated IDs can proceed independently. A backend idempotency endpoint adds hosting, authentication checks, operations work, and its own failure boundary, but can combine authoritative scoring with a durable request-to-result mapping. Its response could return the committed result and identifier, reducing the mobile client's separate confirmation workflow, although a lost response still requires reconciliation. Neither approach makes network timeouts equivalent to cancellation. The backend must atomically bind the key to the payload digest and reject changed payloads, or it merely relocates the duplicate-write problem. For this small assignment, the client transaction is easier to reproduce and inspect. For a graded scoring system, the backend's ability to enforce honest score computation outweighs its extra complexity, provided its replay and authorization rules are tested as carefully as the client recovery path.
